Vignette: Kofi, Age 23

Kofi grew up in Accra, the kind of city he loved precisely because it was always becoming something new — roads widening, markets shifting, neighborhoods reinventing themselves overnight. That restless energy is part of what drew him to urban planning. He moved to London eighteen months ago to take a junior position with a municipal design consultancy, excited to bring ideas back home one day, to build cities that actually served the people living in them.

It happened on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. He was walking back from the office, still carrying his laptop bag, earphones in, thinking through a transit corridor proposal he'd been working on. Three men surrounded him near an underpass about four blocks from his flat. What followed lasted perhaps six minutes, though Kofi still cannot account for the time accurately. He was punched to the ground, kicked repeatedly, and had his bag taken. One of the men held something against his ribs — he still doesn't know whether it was a knife or a finger pressed hard through a jacket — and told him not to move or make a sound. He lay still on the cold concrete long after they were gone, unable to tell whether they had actually left or were simply waiting.

He filed a police report that night. He went to work the following Monday. He told himself he was fine.

Within two weeks, it became clear that he was not. He stopped sleeping in any meaningful way, lying rigid in the dark, listening to the sounds of the building — footsteps in the hallway, a door closing on another floor — and cataloguing each one as a possible threat. When he did sleep, he returned to the underpass. He would wake with his heart hammering, the phantom pressure still against his ribs, and spend the next hour sitting on the edge of his bed with the lights on.

Getting to work became its own ordeal. The route he used to walk without thinking now required negotiation. He began taking the long way around, adding twenty minutes to his commute, because the long way avoided underpasses entirely. Then he started avoiding certain tube stations because the platforms felt too enclosed. He knows, intellectually, that the geometry of a space doesn't determine its danger. He works with geometry for a living. But knowing this does nothing to quiet the alarm that sounds in his chest when he enters a narrow or shadowed space.

At the office, he sits with his back to the wall and his eyes on the door. His colleagues have noticed that he startles easily — a chair scraping across a floor, someone dropping a binder — and he has seen them exchange glances. He used to be the person who stayed late, who brought energy to brainstorming sessions, who genuinely loved talking about how a well-designed public space could make people feel safe. Now he finds it almost unbearable to discuss pedestrian safety or lighting in public areas, topics that once animated him. The irony is not lost on him, and it makes him feel something close to grief.

He has begun to wonder whether the city itself is the problem — whether London specifically has done something to him, or whether he was simply naive to believe that good design could make a place truly safe. He thinks about the underpass proposal he was working on that evening, the one in his stolen bag, and feels a complicated disgust he cannot fully articulate.

He calls his mother in Accra on Sunday evenings but has not told her what happened. He doesn't want her to worry, and he doesn't want to say out loud that he is struggling, because saying it would make it real in a way he is not yet prepared to accept. He is twenty-three years old. He came here to build something. Most days now, he is simply trying to make it from morning to night without falling apart.
